The thermal diffusivity plot shows the values measured in this study at 1273 K as well as the result of the prior three curves as a line. 17 4 Methods and Data Processing 4.1 Thermal Analysis Methods and Uncertainty The liquidus and solidus data points have been determined by thermal analysis using a Mettler-Toledo DSC/TGA2 instrument operating with a high temperature DTA sample carrier mode. Many resources are available that separate and explain the many variants of thermal analysis with the author’s suggestions for further reading being (Brown 2001; Wagner 2009; Sesták 1984). In differential thermal analysis, the furnace temperature changes according to a pre-programmed profile, applying the same system surroundings to a sample and a reference. The temperature difference between the sample and reference is proportional to the differences in reaction heat flow. Temperature difference is converted to heat flow by the software through the calibration methodology. The signal output by the DTA/TGA instrument are heat flow and measured mass as a function of time. The reference temperature and the actual measured sample temperature are also recorded, but the heat flow curves are the primary measurement. The overall heat flow is proportional to the specific heat of the sample (and system). Phase transformations manifest as peaks or valleys in the otherwise smooth heat flow signal as the enthalpy of reaction is expressed or absorbed. The integral of those peaks over the course of the reaction is then the total heat of reaction. While the individual peaks for each reaction are useful in their entirety, specific points taken from those curves are used for the liquidus determination here. These specific points are: 1.) onset of melting during heating, 2.) the peak heat flow during heating, 3.) the endset during heating, and 4.) the onset of solidification which is referred to as the nucleation onset. Only the first two of those quantities are theoretically tied to thermodynamic quantities; however, the last two quantities are extremely useful for providing physical bounds. The onset of melting corresponds to the solidus or at least the solidus confounded by homogenization kinetics. The peak heat flow during heating of a simple binary alloy melting process corresponds to the liquidus. Since measurement of the liquidus by this method contains many confounding factors, as outlined in W. J. Boettinger and Kattner (2002), the endset during heating provides a very useful upper bound because it is a kinetically limited indicator despite the fact that it is not a thermodynamically important point. Similarly, since the nucleation of solid from the liquid requires at least some degree of undercooling, the nucleation temperature during cooling can provide a useful lower bound for the liquidus.
